claims.text: Conventional casting of CoCrFeNiTi produces bulk material with high porosity.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has a homogeneous single-phase structure.
The hardness of conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi is below 200 HV.
High-energy ball milling induces severe plastic deformation and mechanical alloying in CoCrFeNiTi powder.
Milling for 20 hours at a 10:1 ball-to-powder ratio followed by SPS at 900-1000°C is an effective operating regime for the proposed alloy.
The proposed SPS range of 900-1000°C is below the solidus of CoCrFeNiTi.
A heating rate of 100°C/min can manage thermal-expansion mismatch during SPS.
High-energy milling produces a nanocrystalline grain size below 100 nm in this alloy.
High-energy milling produces a high dislocation density in this alloy.
Milling-generated dislocations act as nucleation sites for the FCC phase.
The milling-generated defect structure kinetically suppresses diffusion-dependent HCP formation.
A high SPS heating rate and short dwell trap CoCrFeNiTi in a metastable FCC solid-solution state.
HCP formation in this system is driven by Ti-rich segregation and is associated with brittle behavior.
Applying 50 MPa during SPS eliminates porosity.
The proposed treatment produces a microstructure dominated by FCC with a minor BCC fraction and no HCP phase.
The proposed treatment produces density above 98% of theoretical density.
The treated alloy will exhibit Vickers hardness above 400 HV.
The predicted hardness increase arises from a combination of grain-boundary strengthening and solute drag.
Exceeding an HCP-nucleation temperature threshold or heating too slowly will prevent stabilization of the desired FCC/BCC microstructure.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that slow heating and higher temperature favor HCP formation, so observing more HCP and lower hardness in the slowly heated 1100°C Set B would support, rather than falsify, the proposed kinetic-suppression mechanism.

The outcome attributes hardness to both grain-boundary strengthening and solute drag, whereas the falsification rule treats absence of a hardness increase despite refinement as evidence that solute strengthening is the primary driver. That observation does not establish solute strengthening and is inconsistent with the stated combined attribution.
